title: M,P Errors
notes:
Mean Value and Absolute Error

When a physical quantity is measured repeatedly n times, obtaining values A₁, A₂, ..., A_n, the mean (average) value \bar{A} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i is taken as the best estimate of the true value. The absolute error for each measurement is \Delta A_i = \bar{A} - A_i, representing how far each reading deviates from the mean. Some absolute errors are positive (reading above mean) and some negative (reading below mean). The magnitude |\Delta A_i| tells us the size of deviation regardless of direction.

Mean Absolute Error

The mean absolute error \overline{\Delta A} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |\Delta A_i| gives the average magnitude of random errors in the measurements. It quantifies the spread of individual readings around the mean. A smaller mean absolute error indicates higher precision. For example, if five measurements of length give errors with magnitudes 0.02, 0.01, 0.03, 0.01, 0.02 cm, then \overline{\Delta l} = 0.018 cm ≈ 0.02 cm (rounded to one significant figure, as error estimates themselves are approximate).

Relative Error and Percentage Error

The relative error (also called fractional error) is the ratio of mean absolute error to the mean value: \text{Relative error} = \frac{\overline{\Delta A}}{\bar{A}}. It is a dimensionless number that compares the uncertainty to the size of the measurement. The percentage error is the relative error expressed as a percentage: \text{Percentage error} = \frac{\overline{\Delta A}}{\bar{A}} \times 100\%. For example, if \bar{A} = 50.0 and \overline{\Delta A} = 0.5, then percentage error = (0.5/50.0) × 100% = 1%. A smaller percentage error means the measurement is more reliable relative to its magnitude.

Reporting a Final Measurement

A complete measurement result is reported as: A = \bar{A} \pm \overline{\Delta A}, followed by the appropriate unit. For example: Length l = (5.25 \pm 0.03) cm. This means the true value is expected to lie in the interval [5.22, 5.28] cm. Rules for reporting: (1) The error should be rounded to ONE significant figure (e.g., 0.032 → 0.03). (2) The mean value should be rounded to the same decimal place as the error. (3) Always include units. (4) The percentage error indicates reliability — a 1% error is excellent; a 20% error suggests poor technique or an unsuitable instrument.

Error Propagation in Addition and Subtraction

When a quantity x is calculated from measurements a and b using x = a + b or x = a - b, the maximum absolute error in x is: \Delta x = \Delta a + \Delta b. The errors ADD because the worst case is when both errors go in the same direction. Example: If l = (10.0 \pm 0.1) cm and b = (5.0 \pm 0.1) cm, then l + b = (15.0 \pm 0.2) cm and l - b = (5.0 \pm 0.2) cm. The absolute error increases in both addition and subtraction.

Error Propagation in Multiplication and Division

When x = a \times b or x = a/b, the maximum relative error is the sum of relative errors: \frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}. This follows from taking logarithms: \ln x = \ln a + \ln b (or \ln a - \ln b), then differentiating. Example: If a = (4.0 \pm 0.1) and b = (2.0 \pm 0.1), then x = a \times b = 8.0 and \frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{0.1}{4.0} + \frac{0.1}{2.0} = 0.025 + 0.05 = 0.075. So \Delta x = 0.075 × 8.0 = 0.6. Result: x = 8.0 \pm 0.6.

Error Propagation for Powers

When a quantity is raised to a power, the relative error is multiplied by the exponent. If x = a^n, then \frac{\Delta x}{x} = |n| \cdot \frac{\Delta a}{a}. Example: Volume of a sphere V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r³. The error in V is \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \cdot \frac{\Delta r}{r}. If the radius is measured with 2% error, the volume has 6% error. This rule applies to any power: square root (n = ½) halves the relative error; reciprocal (n = -1) preserves the relative error magnitude.

Combined Error Propagation (General Case)

For a general formula involving multiplication, division, and powers: Q = k \cdot a^p \cdot b^q \cdot c^r (where k is a constant), the maximum percentage error is: \frac{\Delta Q}{Q} \times 100\% = |p|\frac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100\% + |q|\frac{\Delta b}{b} \times 100\% + |r|\frac{\Delta c}{c} \times 100\%. Example: Density \rho = m/V = m/(\frac{4}{3}\pi r³). So \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + 3\frac{\Delta r}{r}. This combined formula handles any algebraic combination of measured quantities.

Accuracy and Precision in Detail

Accuracy refers to how close a measurement is to the true value. High accuracy means small systematic error. Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to each other. High precision means small random error (small spread). A measurement can be: (1) Accurate and precise — clustered near true value. (2) Accurate but not precise — scattered but centered near true value (average is correct). (3) Precise but not accurate — tightly clustered but far from true value (systematic error present). (4) Neither — widely scattered and far from true value. The least count of the instrument determines precision; calibration determines accuracy.

Significant Figures in Calculations

After performing calculations, results must reflect the precision of the input data. Addition/Subtraction rule: Round to the fewest decimal places among inputs. Example: 12.34 + 5.6 = 17.94 → 17.9 (limited by 5.6 with 1 decimal). Multiplication/Division rule: Round to the fewest significant figures among inputs. Example: 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6 (limited by 2.5 with 2 sig figs). Mixed operations: Apply the appropriate rule at each step, or keep extra digits and round only at the end. In NEB exams, showing the significant figure rule application earns partial credit.
confusion: Absolute error in addition is additive; relative error in multiplication is additive — This is the single most common source of calculation errors. Remember: \Delta(a+b) = \Delta a + \Delta b, but \Delta(ab)/(ab) = \Delta a/a + \Delta b/b.

When squaring or cubing, multiply the RELATIVE error by the exponent — If \Delta r/r = 2%, then \Delta(r²)/r² = 2\times 2% = 4% and \Delta(r³)/r³ = 3\times 2% = 6%. Never forget to multiply by the power.

Percentage error can exceed 100% for very small measurements — If measuring a thin wire with a ruler (LC = 1 mm), the error can be larger than the measurement itself. This signals that the instrument is unsuitable, not that the formula is wrong.

Significant figures reflect PRECISION, not accuracy — Reporting 5.00 cm (3 sig figs) means you're confident to \pm 0.01 cm, but the true value could be 5.05 cm (accurate?) — that's a separate question about calibration.

When subtracting nearly equal numbers, you LOSE significant figures — Example: 5.00 - 4.98 = 0.02. Two measurements with 3 sig figs yield a result with only 1 sig fig! This 'catastrophic cancellation' is why difference measurements need high-precision instruments.

The mean absolute error is rounded to ONE significant figure — Even if calculation gives 0.0347 cm, report it as \pm 0.03 cm. The mean value is then rounded to match the decimal place: 12.457 cm → 12.46 cm. Don't report more digits in error than justified.
Relative error is dimensionless but percentage error has a '%' sign — They are the same number conceptually; percentage error is just relative error \times 100. A 0.05 relative error = 5% error.

Systematic errors do NOT average out with repeated measurements — Taking 100 readings of a mis-calibrated scale gives 100 equally wrong values. Only random errors reduce by \sqrt{n} averaging; systematic errors require calibration correction.
practice: The temperature of two bodies is measured as T₁ = (40 \pm 1)°C and T₂ = (100 \pm 1)°C. Find the temperature difference and its error. [Solution: \Delta T = T₂ - T₁ = 60°C. \Delta(\Delta T) = \Delta T₂ + \Delta T₁ = 1 + 1 = 2°C. Answer: (60 \pm 2)°C.]

The mass and volume of a body are m = (5.00 \pm 0.05) kg and V = (1.00 \pm 0.05) \times 10⁻³ m³. Find density and its percentage error. [Solution: \rho = m/V = 5.00/1.00\times10⁻³ = 5000 kg/m³. \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{0.05}{5.00} + \frac{0.05}{1.00} = 0.01 + 0.05 = 0.06 = 6\%. \Delta \rho = 0.06 \times 5000 = 300 kg/m³. Answer: \rho = (5000 \pm 300) kg/m³.]

The radius of a sphere is r = (2.5 \pm 0.1) cm. Find its volume and the percentage error. [Solution: V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}(3.1416)(15.625) = 65.45 cm³. \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = 3 \times \frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.12 = 12\%. \Delta V = 0.12 \times 65.45 = 7.85 \approx 8 cm³. Answer: V = (65 \pm 8) cm³.]

Two resistors R₁ = (10 \pm 0.5) \Omega and R₂ = (20 \pm 0.5) \Omega are connected in parallel. Find equivalent resistance and its error. [Solution: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20. R = 20/3 = 6.67 \Omega. For parallel: \frac{\Delta R}{R} = \frac{R}{R_1^2}\Delta R_1 + \frac{R}{R_2^2}\Delta R_2 \approx simplified: \frac{\Delta R}{R} \approx \frac{\Delta R_1}{R_1} + \frac{\Delta R_2}{R_2} = 0.05 + 0.025 = 0.075. \Delta R = 0.075 \times 6.67 \approx 0.5 \Omega. Answer: R = (6.7 \pm 0.5) \Omega.]

The period T of a pendulum is (2.0 \pm 0.05) s and length l = (1.00 \pm 0.02) m. Find g = 4\pi²l/T² and its error. [Solution: g = 4(3.1416)²(1.00)/(2.0)² = 39.48/4.0 = 9.87 m/s². \frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta l}{l} + 2\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{0.02}{1.00} + 2\frac{0.05}{2.0} = 0.02 + 0.05 = 0.07 = 7\%. \Delta g = 0.07 \times 9.87 = 0.69 \approx 0.7 m/s². Answer: g = (9.9 \pm 0.7) m/s².]

A rectangular block has dimensions l = (15.0 \pm 0.1) cm, b = (10.0 \pm 0.1) cm, h = (5.0 \pm 0.1) cm. Find volume and maximum percentage error. [Solution: V = 15.0 \times 10.0 \times 5.0 = 750 cm³. \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{0.1}{15.0} + \frac{0.1}{10.0} + \frac{0.1}{5.0} = 0.0067 + 0.01 + 0.02 = 0.0367 = 3.67\%. \Delta V = 0.0367 \times 750 = 27.5 \approx 28 cm³. Answer: V = (750 \pm 28) cm³ or (7.5 \pm 0.3) \times 10² cm³.]

Five students measure the acceleration due to gravity and obtain: 9.78, 9.82, 9.75, 9.80, 9.85 m/s². Find the mean value, mean absolute error, and relative error. [Solution: Mean \bar{g} = (9.78+9.82+9.75+9.80+9.85)/5 = 49.00/5 = 9.80 m/s². Absolute errors: 0.02, 0.02, 0.05, 0.00, 0.05. Mean absolute error = (0.02+0.02+0.05+0.00+0.05)/5 = 0.14/5 = 0.028 \approx 0.03 m/s². Relative error = 0.03/9.80 = 0.0031 = 0.31%. Answer: g = (9.80 \pm 0.03) m/s².]

The refractive index of glass is measured as n = 1.50 \pm 0.02. If the angle of incidence is i = 30.0° \pm 0.5°, find the angle of refraction r and its error using Snell's law. [Solution: n = sin i/sin r \Rightarrow sin r = sin 30°/1.50 = 0.5/1.50 = 0.3333. r = arcsin(0.3333) = 19.47°. For error: \frac{\Delta r}{\cos r} = \cos i \cdot \frac{\Delta n}{n} + \sin i \cdot \frac{\Delta i}{n} (approx). This requires calculus; for NEB, focus on simple propagation: \frac{\Delta n}{n} = 0.02/1.50 = 1.33%.]

The resistance of a wire is R = \rho l/A where \rho = (1.0 \pm 0.05) \times 10⁻⁶ \Omega\cdotm, l = (2.0 \pm 0.02) m, A = (3.0 \pm 0.1) \times 10⁻⁷ m². Find R and percentage error. [Solution: R = \rho l/A = (1.0\times10⁻⁶)(2.0)/(3.0\times10⁻⁷) = 20/3 = 6.67 \Omega. \frac{\Delta R}{R} = \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} + \frac{\Delta l}{l} + \frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{0.05}{1.0} + \frac{0.02}{2.0} + \frac{0.1}{3.0} = 0.05 + 0.01 + 0.033 = 0.093 = 9.3\%. \Delta R = 0.093 \times 6.67 = 0.62 \approx 0.6 \Omega. Answer: R = (6.7 \pm 0.6) \Omega.]

The kinetic energy of a body is KE = \frac{1}{2}mv² with m = (2.0 \pm 0.1) kg and v = (3.0 \pm 0.1) m/s. Find KE and its error. [Solution: KE = \frac{1}{2}(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J. \frac{\Delta KE}{KE} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + 2\frac{\Delta v}{v} = \frac{0.1}{2.0} + 2\frac{0.1}{3.0} = 0.05 + 0.067 = 0.117 = 11.7\%. \Delta KE = 0.117 \times 9.0 = 1.05 \approx 1.1 J. Answer: KE = (9.0 \pm 1.1) J.]
universalFacts: The concept of 'mean absolute error' was formalized by Adrien-Marie Legendre (1805) and Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809) — Gauss showed that minimizing the sum of squared errors (least squares method) yields the maximum likelihood estimate when errors follow a normal distribution, which is why we use standard deviation rather than mean absolute error in advanced statistics.

NEB exam tip: For percentage error in g using a pendulum (g = 4\pi²l/T²), the error in T is DOUBLED because T appears squared — This is why timing many oscillations (not just one) is crucial; it reduces \Delta T/T significantly, and the doubling effect becomes less damaging.

Error propagation rules apply to ANY differentiable function — For Q = f(a,b,c,...), the general formula is \Delta Q = \sqrt{(\partial f/\partial a \cdot \Delta a)^2 + (\partial f/\partial b \cdot \Delta b)^2 + ...} (root-sum-square method). The 'addition of errors' taught here is the conservative upper bound (worst-case scenario).

The 68-95-99.7 rule in statistics connects to error reporting — One standard deviation \sigma covers ~68% of measurements; reporting \bar{A} \pm \sigma means ~68% confidence. In Class 11 NEB, \pm is treated as the total range (best case to worst case), giving wider intervals.

Systematic errors shift ALL measurements in the same direction — If a stopwatch runs slow by 5%, every time measurement is 5% too large. This cannot be detected by taking more readings; it requires calibration against a standard (e.g., atomic clock). Students often overlook systematic errors in experiments.

Modern particle physics reports statistical and systematic errors SEPARATELY — Example: Higgs boson mass = 125.35 \pm 0.15 (stat) \pm 0.06 (syst) GeV. The first error shrinks with more data; the second does not. NEB questions focus only on random error treatment, but awareness of this distinction is valuable for university-level physics.

The rule for error in powers (multiply relative error by exponent) comes from logarithmic differentiation — If Q = a^n, then ln Q = n ln a, and dQ/Q = n \cdot da/a. This is the same mathematical principle behind the error propagation for any power law relationship in science.
